chunks: Humayd ibn Ziyad from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah from someone else from Aban, and Muhammad ibn Yahya from Abdullah ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Aban from Ismail al-Fadl al-Hashimi who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the forced labor in the villages and what is taken from the porters and the hired workers in the villages, so he said: 'Stipulate upon them. So whatever you stipulate upon them from the dirhams and the forced labor, and whatever is besides that, then it is for you, and it is not for you to take anything from it until you have stipulated to them beforehand, even though you are certain that every one who lodges in that village takes that from him.'

He said: 'And I asked him about a man who built houses or a house in his right of easement next to his neighbor, so the people of the house became his neighbors. Is it for him to repulse them while they are unwilling?' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'They are free; they lodge wherever they wish and move wherever they wish.'

key_terms.يَرُدَّهُمْ: To repulse or turn them away

ai.seo_question: What are the conditions for imposing forced labor and lodging on non-Muslims in Islamic jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the fiqh of sukhr (forced labor) and lodging, emphasizing that while these obligations are customary for non-Muslims (ahl al-dhimma), they are not absolute until explicitly stipulated, reflecting the Shia principle of contractual certainty in fiscal duties. It further establishes the right of free movement and residence, noting that neighbors cannot be forcibly evicted, which underscores the balance between state rights and individual property rights in Islamic governance.
